headline.main: Photographing the Suffering in Gaza: A Palestinian Photojournalist Finds Himself at the Center of Controversy
headline.social: Photographing the Suffering in Gaza: A Palestinian Photojournalist Finds Himself at the Center of Controversy

intro: Anas Fteiha works as a photojournalist in the Gaza Strip. A photo of him taking pictures of people waiting for food at an aid distribution site caught the attention of a tabloid in far-away Germany. Now, the Palestinian is scared for his life.
text:
Photographers usually remain in the background. In the Gaza Strip, they point their cameras at people who are mourning loved ones, living in the rubble of destroyed buildings or standing in lines waiting in vain for something to eat. The Palestinian photojournalist Anas Fteiha has photographed many such scenes, including on July 24 in the Ansar neighborhood of Gaza City, where he was taking photos for the Turkish state-owned newswire Anadolu.
For the past several weeks, he has been the target of a campaign as a result of the photos he took that day. Triggered by an article published in the German tabloid Bild and fueled by official Israeli government channels, Fteiha himself has now become the focus of attention. The 31-year-old even fears for his life, as he told DER SPIEGEL over the phone.
What happened? Shortly before the Bild article was published, the influential Munich-based daily Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) published a picture of Fteiha showing him shooting photos of starving civilians in Gaza. The headline read: "How Authentic Are the Photos from Gaza?” The article included the following sentence: "There are indeed photos of people holding empty pots in Gaza that show that they aren’t standing in front of a food distribution site, but only in front of a photographer.” The picture of Fteiha served to illustrate the article, but he wasn’t mentioned by name in the piece.
Two days later, Bild published an article  under the headline "This Gaza Photographer Stages Hamas Propaganda” – and the tabloid used the same photo showing Fteiha taking pictures of Gaza civilians standing with empty pots in front of a makeshift metal barrier. The photo caption reads: "Gaza photographer Anas Zayed Fteiha stages the real suffering of the Palestinians for the global public – for the benefit of Hamas and its propaganda.”
The Israeli President Gets Involved
On August 6, the Israeli Embassy in Berlin wrote on X : "Be careful of Fake News! A joint reporting project by @SZ & @BILD shows: Hamas is using staged photos – known as "Pallywood” – to manipulate global opinion. At the center of the effort is Anas Fteiha, a radical Islamist photographer from Gaza, whose photos have been used by CNN, BBC and Reuters – despite being obvious propaganda (…) What we are seeing isn’t reporting – it is staging.”
Numerous Israeli media outlets seized on the doubts surrounding Anas Fteiha’s photos. In reference to the article in the Süddeutsche Zeitung – which requested, in response to a query from DER SPIEGEL, "to keep the reporting of the Süddeutsche Zeitung and that of Bild strictly separate – the newspaper Times of Israel wrote : "The report alleged that some photos showing Gazans with empty pots were not taken at food distribution centers, as widely assumed and stated, but were instead staged in front of photographers to create the illusion of desperation.”
Even Israeli President Isaac Herzog held the image of Anas Fteiha up to the cameras at a conference in Estonia  and referred to investigative reports from leading German newspapers. "It was all staged,” Herzog said, exposing the "hypocrisy and manipulation” of Hamas.
Whereas the article in the Süddeutsche Zeitung posed the broader question as to which images from Gaza can be trusted and where doubts are warranted, the article in Bild focused on Fteiha and his presumed political views. The accusation: "The staging of suffering (…) frequently benefits Hamas and its propaganda.”
The writers reference the "reporting by the Süddeutsche Zeitung,” which calls into question precisely such images: "Emaciated children, desperate mothers and people begging for food with empty pots.”
Bild writes: "The hunger is (almost always) real – but the photos may not be.” The tabloid accuses Fteiha of having held back some of the photos he took on July 24. The writers of the article suggest that could be because those images primarily show men who presumably received food, as shown, the paper claims, by the pictures taken by other photographers. The article raises the question as to whether Fteiha perhaps had no use for such photos.
Whereas the Süddeutsche Zeitung said in response to a DER SPIEGEL query that it had never sought to contact Fteiha, Bild told DER SPIEGEL that the photographer hadn’t responded to a query sent to him. That is also what the article in Bild claims. Fteiha rejects that characterization.
Since the publication of the Bild article, Fteiha has been unable to shake the accusation that he staged the scene in question – and it has changed his life. What, though, really did happen on that July day in Gaza City? We took a closer look.
Fteiha Was Apparently at a Field Kitchen
An Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) investigation – the examination of publicly available sources, including those on the internet – performed by DER SPIEGEL found that Fteiha was indeed standing at a field kitchen in the photo in question. On one of the photos he took that day, a banner is visible with the name of the field kitchen in question: Khaula al-Badri. It is operated by the Palestinian aid organization Khair al-Nisa, which documents its activities on Instagram.
The Süddeutsche Zeitung article shows the photo of Anas Fteiha and quotes Gerhard Paul, a professor emeritus of history and an expert on photography. He voices a fundamental skepticism of photos from war zones like Gaza. He doesn’t specifically address the Fteiha photo, but does discuss images of similar scenes: "Where is the photographer standing? What is he surrounded by?” he asks. "What are the people depicted in the image looking at? Are they looking at what we assume they are looking at, a food distribution site, for example? Or are they looking at a phalanx of photographers?”
In conclusion, the Süddeutsche Zeitung writes: "There are indeed photos of people with empty pots in Gaza which show that they aren’t standing in front of a food distribution site, but in front of a photographer.”
When contacted, the Süddeutsche Zeitung admitted that it "has become clear” that the question posed in its headline – "How Authentic Are the Photos from Gaza?” – "was apparently linked to the scene in the photo used to illustrate the article.” Namely, the photo showing Anas Fteiha standing in front of people holding empty pots. The "comments from the expert Paul also discusses such a scene as an example.” From today’s perspective, the Süddeutsche Zeitung wrote to DER SPIEGEL, it would have been better to ask Anas Fteiha himself how that specific photo came to pass.
Back to the situation on July 24. The OSINT investigation determined that the food wasn’t prepared in the forecourt, which was delineated by the makeshift metal barrier and was where Fteiha and others were standing, but in a covered area behind it. There are numerous additional photos showing Fteiha on that day in a number of other positions, allowing for a better view of the scene in its entirety.
With clear information regarding location, time and individuals, additional reference images and videos of the field kitchen can be pinpointed using a Google reverse image search. They are characterized by a number of recurring details: The red-and-white barrier, the pattern of the buildings in the background, the metal rack for the pots, the gate with its blue tarps and the NGO employees present at the scene.
Taken together, these indications suggest that there can be no question of the photo in question being staged. The food distribution site has been in operation at least since the middle of July 2025.
In response to the query from DER SPIEGEL, Bild responded that its article never asserted that there was no field kitchen at the site nor did it say the photo was posed. The staging, Bild wrote, comes from the careful selection of the photos, with the printed photo showing him in a situation in which only adult men (and no food) were in front of his camera. "Photos taken by Anas Fteiha of this scene were never published anywhere, according to our reporting, and are also not available on Anadolu, in contrast to the photos of other photojournalists,” Bild wrote. The article expresses the supposition that Fteiha’s photos were carefully selected to show "chaos and destruction.” "And especially: children, mothers, suffering in close-up and in perfect lighting conditions.”
Fteiha’s Was Commissioned That Day by His Agency
It is true that Anas Fteiha didn’t publish a single one of his own images from the scene in which he was photographed squatting down before a crowd made up mostly of men. But he had already made the reasons for that public on July 26 on his Instagram feed , prior to the appearance of the articles in the Süddeutsche Zeitung and Bild. The state-owned Turkish news agency had commissioned him and others to photograph a story about hunger from their own perspectives, says Fteiha.
They had been asked to document "the suffering of displaced Palestinians in their struggle to access food,” as he writes on Instagram on July 26, "while often experiencing hunger himself.” Which is why he appears in the photos taken on that day.
The photo essay  showing Fteiha and his colleagues at work was published by the Anadolu press agency on the evening of July 24 – along with a video of food distribution  showing Fteiha as meals are distributed to the waiting Gazans. At one point, he jumps to his feet because of the chaotic nature of the distribution. Yellow liquid slops over the rim of the pots as the people yell.
Gaza Is in the Grip of Famine
On top of all that, Fteiha apparently has no problem with the photo showing mostly men standing in front of him with empty pots. He published it on his own Instagram channel on July 26, and it shows the entire background of the food distribution site. Bild still hadn’t published that photo on its website one-and-a-half weeks later.
There is also a photo showing him apparently taking a picture of a child who has received food.
Ultimately, a clear picture emerges: Anas Fteiha was clearly on site at the food distribution center. These images and numerous other photos on social media also plainly show that numerous women and children were also waiting for food on that day, and not just "primarily adult men,” as Bild wrote.
Furthermore, people waiting for food in Gaza with empty pots is an increasingly frequent sight in Gaza. According to experts from the respected Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), one part of the Gaza Strip is now suffering from famine, as a report from last Friday shows. The area in question is in the northern part of the Gaza Strip and includes Gaza City. This new phase is characterized by "starvation, destitution and death,” says the IPC, adding that more than half a million people are affected.
Given this situation, photographers in Gaza don’t have to search for long to take pictures of the suffering, nor must they herd people together to stage such images, says Fteiha. "Waiting in front of the field kitchens is part of daily life in Gaza. There is far too little food for far too many people, so residents are forced to stand in line for hours. Some return home with empty pots.”
Fteiha Is a Well-Known Photographer with No Known Ties to Hamas
Our OSINT investigation clearly shows that Fteiha was on site as a professional photographer. He can be seen on public social media channels, and he published his photos under his own name. Fteiha works for respected press agencies, with his images distributed by Getty Images, among others. A search using the filter "Gaza City” over a 30-day time period in early August turned up more than 4,200 images from a number of different photographers – with many of them showing precisely this food distribution site.
In most cases, the verification of photos from Gaza is difficult and uncertainties often remain. Because Israel has denied journalists access to the Gaza Strip from the very beginning of the war, news outlets, including DER SPIEGEL, are forced to turn to publicly available sources. As soon as questions arise about the provenance of images, they are checked with the greatest of care.
The first step is always a search for reference photos: Images of the same even taken by different people from different angles. In Gaza, the destruction in many places is so significant that there are hardly any identifiable structures or landmarks to provide orientation.
Of equal importance is the question as to who produced the material in question. Numerous photos and videos are circulating on the internet, the age, origins and authenticity of which are frequently unclear. In addition to professional photographers, NGO workers, activists, eyewitnesses and officials in Gaza also publish their photos on the web – and they all have different motives.
It is often extremely difficult to come up with a reliable judgment, a process that can include photo analyses, the comparison of contextual information, reverse image searches, comparisons with current and past satellite imagery and research on social media channels.
What Role Does Hamas Play?
The expert quoted by the Süddeutsche Zeitung, Gerhard Paul, has been researching photography from Israel and Gaza for 25 years and has traveled to the region himself. He claimed that the images have an "additional function.” "They are intended to overwrite the brutal images from the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023. Many no longer remember those pictures. Hamas is masterful at staging images.”
Paul said that he often no longer even looks at the images from Gaza, but nevertheless hypothesized: "The Palestinian side is primarily interested in the emotionalization of the pacifist, Western societies. And it is working extremely well.”
Daniel Etter is an award-winning photographer who has also traveled to war zones on behalf of DER SPIEGEL. He says such claims are "an attempt to discredit the work of all photographers in Gaza.”
Etter keeps close track of the photos coming from Gaza. "This discourse is absurd, as if anything has to be staged in Gaza. In such areas that are home to catastrophe, photographers don’t have to stage anything.” It is quite possible that Hamas limits the access of photographers, he says, noting that functionaries, military positions and fighters cannot be seen in the photos currently coming out of Gaza. But that doesn’t lessen the suffering depicted by the images. "That is genuine in Gaza.”
Dirk Gebhardt, 55, a photojournalist and professor of photojournalism and documentary photography at the Dortmund University of Applied Sciences and Arts, takes a similar view. "Each party to the conflict, whether it is Hamas or Israel, has a political interest,” he says. Hamas, says Gebhardt, is well known for pressuring journalists. "People who don’t cooperate and who oppose Hamas are beaten and tortured. But that doesn’t mean that the photographer who took the photo didn’t report as authentically as possible.”
Palestinian Journalists Are Under Pressure from Many Different Sides
On top of that is the fact that Palestinian journalists, in particular, are targeted by criticism. "With his claim that it is a scene staged by Hamas, Netanyahu wants to distract from the fact that he is violating international law. It is a self-protective claim to divert attention from his own crimes. If Western journalists were on the ground, it would be far more difficult to undermine their credibility than it is Palestinians,” says Gebhardt.
But what is to make of the accusation made by Bild that Fteiha wrote "Fuck Israel” in an Instagram video from January 25, 2025? He doesn’t deny the post, but says: "Sorry, but I don’t love anyone who bombs me for 22 months. I would never hate anyone because of their faith, but because of the injustice that takes place on a daily basis in Gaza.” Israel, he says, has taken half of his friends from him during the war. "I have something against people who occupy my country in the name of religion.”
Fteiha is referring to demands by the right-wing extremist members of Netanyahu’s coalition to reoccupy Gaza. Politicians like Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister for national security, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister who is also responsible for settlement policy, are convinced that all of Israel – including Gaza – was promised to the Jewish people by God and thus belongs to them. Even Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently expressed support for the vision of a "Greater Israel.”
In other words, it should come has no surprise that Palestinian journalists don’t have much sympathy for Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip. Fteiha also shares on Instagram posts from the Europe Palestine Network, which publishes anti-Israeli content. But that doesn’t necessarily have to mean that he has ties to Hamas or is even a member.
DER SPIEGEL works together with Palestinian journalists in Gaza who also report on protests against Hamas in the Gaza Strip – despite the dangers inherent in doing so.
The Consequences for Fteiha’s Life
The situation for journalists in Gaza is fundamentally different from those who report in free and peaceful environments. Even as Palestinian photographers document the daily suffering in the war zone, they are also personally affected by the bombardments and by the pressure exerted on them by the state. They document hunger and destruction while they, too, are also suffering from hunger and destruction. That doesn’t automatically make the images they produce less authentic.
A comprehensive understanding of the situation also requires a look to Israel. The media journalist Oren Persico recently said in an interview with DER SPIEGEL that the large Israeli media outlets – with the exception of the liberal newspaper Haaretz – reports sparingly on the hunger and deaths in the Gaza Strip. Many Israeli journalists, he said, learned their "job as conscripts from army radio,” such that they become "used to limitations from the very beginning, such as the censorship of reports on military operations.” In the case of the current war, however, he said he believes it is "mainly self-censorship.”
When Fteiha realized that he had become the focus of a campaign, he says he didn’t initially realize the extent of it. "I then did a bit of research and realized that Bild has a clearly pro-Israeli stance.” When Israeli President Isaac Herzog then publicly mentioned the image, the story began making the rounds in Gaza. Since then, he says, he has felt the consequences of the two German newspaper stories every day. "People are distancing themselves from me. I no longer sleep together with my family so as not to endanger them.” What really bothers him, though, is the question as to how people can seriously seek to minimize the horror of what is happening in Gaza.
He says he is concerned that he will no longer receive any commissions as a photojournalist. His family depends on the money he earns. He says he tries not to think too much about it, but if he is being honest, he adds, he is afraid – particularly after the targeted killing of the Al-Jazeera correspondent Anas Al-Sharif and his colleagues by an Israeli drone strike. Israeli army spokespersons laid the rhetorical groundwork ahead of Sharif’s killing. "Is my death currently being prepared?” wonders Fteiha.
Ten minutes after the conversation comes to an end, Fteiha calls again. He wants to say one last thing, he says. "If anything happens to me or my family, then these German media outlets bear the responsibility.” When confronted with these comments, Bild responded by saying that it doesn’t comment on responses to its reporting. The Süddeutsche Zeitung wrote that it of course finds it extremely concerning.
